title: AI performance meets the test of evidence
subtitle: Revised research brief · First online 26 October–1 November 2026
lead: Correction dated 6 November 2026. This edition separates verifiable new journal publications from older or presently unverified citations, with direct original-source links and explicit evidence limits. The original briefing contained twelve citations; seven have individually verified first-online dates in the target week.

publications.contribution: Analyzes how generative-AI randomized trials report technical and operational details.
publications.main_finding: Across 74 reports representing 73 randomized trials, key reporting gaps included algorithm versioning (17/74 reported), input-data eligibility (3/73), and input quality handling (0/72).
publications.evidence_boundary: These are reporting-adherence findings, not direct estimates of the safety or clinical effectiveness of the 73 interventions; the review did not assess trial risk of bias.

publications.contribution: Umbrella review of 50 reviews encompassing 387 primary fracture-detection studies, with 21 meta-analyses contributing to a second-order meta-analysis.
publications.main_finding: Pooled AI sensitivity was 0.897 and specificity 0.904, but most outcome certainty was low or very low; no included review reported adverse events or other safety outcomes.
publications.evidence_boundary: Comparative evidence for AI, clinicians and AI-assisted clinicians was sparse and inconclusive; pooled diagnostic accuracy is not proof of improved patient outcomes.

publications.contribution: Develops the 10-domain OMNI rubric and pilots it with 15 clinician assessors across four health care scenarios and 250 input-output pairs.
publications.main_finding: OMNI differentiated output strengths and weaknesses; fine-grained pairwise agreement across four-point ratings ranged from 30.8% to 53.4%, while broader collapsed agreement was higher.
publications.evidence_boundary: An expert-led pilot with modest fine-grained agreement does not establish broad reliability, psychometric validity or clinical safety across settings.

publications.contribution: Observational cohort analysis of 983,154 patient-portal message responses distinguishes organization-level adoption of an AI drafting tool from actual message-level use.
publications.main_finding: Tool adoption was associated with an 8.6% longer turnaround time, whereas actual tool use was associated with a 29.5% shorter turnaround; there was no overall reduction in after-hours replying.
publications.evidence_boundary: Associations are observational, not randomized causal effects; after-hours results differed by when messages arrived and were sensitive to working-hours definitions.

publications.contribution: Introduces a reusable event-level particle-collision foundation model across downstream physics tasks.
publications.main_finding: EVENET is pretrained on simulated collisions and evaluated on multiple searches and a CMS open-data demonstration.
publications.evidence_boundary: Transfer results are limited to evaluated physics tasks, simulation conditions and measured data.

publications.contribution: Proposes a calibration approach to align aggregate LLM responses more closely with human sample distributions.
publications.main_finding: The study evaluates sample calibration as a correction for discrepancies between LLM and reference human responses.
publications.evidence_boundary: Agreement after calibration is conditional on reference populations and evaluated settings.

publications.contribution: Proposes a human-intention-based analytical framework for attributing AI-related responsibility.
publications.main_finding: The perspective traces accountability through model objectives, training, deployment and oversight decisions.
publications.evidence_boundary: It is a conceptual legal and governance argument, not evidence that proposed rules have been adopted.

signals.title: Benchmark results do not replace patient-relevant evidence
signals.body: Across 74 reports from 73 medical GenAI randomized trials, a reporting audit found algorithm versions documented in just 17/74 reports and no input-quality handling in 72 applicable reports. A separate fracture-detection umbrella review reported pooled sensitivity of 0.897 and specificity of 0.904, but generally low evidence certainty and no reported safety outcomes. The 10-domain OMNI rubric pilot offered structured expert evaluation, yet fine-grained pairwise agreement was only 30.8%–53.4%.
signals.takeaway: Track technical reproducibility, inter-rater reliability, comparative patient-relevant outcomes and safety reporting separately from headline model accuracy.

signals.title: Adoption and individual use are different estimands
signals.body: A cohort study of 983,154 portal-message responses found an 8.6% longer turnaround associated with adopting an AI drafting tool but a 29.5% shorter turnaround associated with its actual use for individual messages. There was no overall decline in after-hours replies, although associations varied across message categories and timing. These estimates are observational, not causal treatment effects.
signals.takeaway: Separate organizational adoption from message-level use, and report the mixed after-hours findings rather than equating speed with reduced clinician burden.

signals.title: A shared scientific model still needs task-specific validation
signals.body: An event-level particle physics foundation model was pretrained on large-scale simulated collisions and evaluated on several downstream tasks, including a CMS open-data demonstration. This offers evidence of transfer in the assessed settings without proving unrestricted generalization.
signals.takeaway: Look for independent data transfer, physical validation and failure modes, not only parameter scale.

signals.title: Useful AI outputs require calibration and accountable human choices
signals.body: An LLM sample-calibration study attempts to better align model-generated responses with human distributions. A PNAS perspective instead emphasizes the human decisions embedded in objectives, training and deployment. The first supplies context-dependent modeling evidence; the second advances a normative framework.
signals.takeaway: Do not confuse sample agreement with population validity, or an accountability proposal with enacted policy.

watchlist: Which clinical evaluations will report prospective patient outcomes, safety and reproducible model versions?
Can calibrated LLM response distributions remain valid across populations and model updates?
How often do physics foundation models transfer successfully to real measurements?
What independent evidence would turn conceptual AI accountability rules into implementable governance?

coverage.notes: This retrospective correction reclassifies the 12 DOI citations in the original Issue 002, NOT a comprehensive sweep of 88 target journals. Seven publisher-dated journal papers first appeared during 26 Oct–1 Nov; three Management Science papers first appeared in December 2025, February 2026 or August 2026 and are historical. PubMed records for the two Science Advances studies report article dates of 28 and 30 October 2026, but their publisher pages returned HTTP 403 during source checking; they remain pending publisher-original verification and are not counted as verified new publications. No independently approved significant development is claimed. Verified complete publisher catalog coverage remains 0/88.

scope: Corrections dated 6 November 2026; the historical 4 November issue date and report URL are preserved. Reclassification covers the twelve original DOI citations only, including three older studies and two Science Advances papers with independently indexed but not directly publisher-verified dates. Study-level methods, numerators, effect estimates and limitations are drawn from linked publisher source abstracts and article text; cross-paper signals are editorial synthesis, not independently reproduced causal analyses. No exhaustive 88-journal discovery, publisher byte-snapshot authentication, independent full-text validation of every study, or authenticated editor receipt is claimed.
